t: Turn one idea into posts for every platform
d: Write one rough idea and get a LinkedIn post, an Instagram caption, a Facebook post and a short video hook, each in the right style.
when: Whenever you have something worth sharing

steps.h: Jot down the idea in plain words
steps.b: In your notes app, write two or three sentences about the news, tip or story. Don't polish it, just get the point down.

steps.h: Ask your AI assistant to adapt it
steps.b: Open ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini and paste this prompt with your idea.
steps.p: I run [type of business] for [audience]. Here is a rough idea I want to share: [your idea]. Turn it into: 1) a LinkedIn post (120-180 words, a strong first line, short paragraphs, end with a question); 2) an Instagram caption (under 100 words, friendly, 5 relevant hashtags at the end); 3) a Facebook post (conversational, under 80 words, with a clear call to action: [what you want people to do]); 4) three opening lines for a 30-second video. Use British English, no hype words, and keep the facts exactly as I gave them.

steps.b: Read each version aloud and change anything you wouldn't say. Ask the assistant to 'make it more casual' or 'shorter' if a version feels off.
Copy each version into its app. Most platforms let you schedule a post for later if you'd rather spread them across the week.

example: LinkedIn: 'Most of our customers ask the same question in their first week...' Instagram: 'The one thing we wish every new customer knew...' +#smallbusiness #tips. Facebook: 'Quick tip from the team: ... Pop in on Saturday and we'll show you.' Video hooks: 'Stop doing this in week one.'
tips: Save the prompt in your notes app with your business details filled in, so next time you only paste the idea.
Check any facts, prices or dates before posting; the assistant can quietly change them.

actions.detail: Write platform-specific versions of the idea
Save all versions in one note for review
Tell the user the drafts are ready to check

t: Fill a month of social posts in one sitting
d: A ready-to-use content calendar in a spreadsheet with dates, themes, captions and image ideas for a whole month of posts.
when: Last week of each month

steps.b: Write down next month's events, offers, launches, holidays and anything seasonal for your customers. Five or six items is plenty.

steps.h: Ask for a calendar as a table
steps.b: Paste this into your AI assistant with your details.
steps.p: Create a social media content calendar for [month and year] for [business name], a [type of business] serving [audience]. We post [number] times a week on [platforms]. Key dates and offers: [list]. Mix the posts roughly 40% helpful tips, 30% behind the scenes, 20% customer stories, 10% offers. Output a table with columns: Date, Day, Platform, Theme, Post caption (under 60 words), Image or video idea, Call to action. Use British English and no hype words.

steps.b: Copy the table and paste it into a new Google Sheet. It usually lands in neat columns; if not, ask the assistant to give it as comma-separated text and use Paste special.
Add a column called Status with options like Idea, Drafted, Scheduled, Posted, so you can see your progress at a glance.

example: Tue 3 Mar | Instagram | Tip | 'Three ways to make your lunch break count...' | Flat lay of a packed lunch | Save this for later. Fri 6 Mar | Facebook | Offer | 'Mother's Day gift sets now in...' | Gift set on shop counter | Order by 25 March.
tips: Keep last month's sheet and tell the assistant which posts did best, so next month leans into what works.

actions.detail: Ask the user for next month's key dates and offers
Build the month's content calendar
Add each post as a row with status Idea

t: Schedule a week of Instagram and Facebook posts at once
d: Design your images in Canva, write captions with AI and queue a full week of Instagram and Facebook posts in about half an hour.
when: Once a week, same time each week

steps.b: Choose three to five topics from your content calendar or from questions customers asked this week.

steps.h: Write the captions in one go
steps.b: Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Write [number] Instagram and Facebook captions for [business name], a [type of business]. Topics: [list topics]. For each: a first line that makes people stop scrolling, 40-80 words, one clear call to action, and 3-5 hashtags that real customers in [your area or niche] would search. Also suggest a short headline (max 6 words) to put on the image. Number them and use British English.

steps.b: Open a Canva Instagram post template, add your headline, then duplicate the page for each post so they all match. Download them as PNGs.

steps.h: Schedule them in Meta Business Suite
steps.b: Open Meta Business Suite (free for linked Facebook Pages and Instagram business accounts), create a post, add the image and caption, choose both Facebook and Instagram, and pick a date and time to schedule.

example: Mon 8am: 'Your boiler is trying to tell you something.' + image 'Winter boiler check'. Wed 12pm: 'Meet Sam, who's been with us 6 years...' Fri 5pm: 'This weekend only: free gas safety check with every service.' All queued in Business Suite.
tips: If your Canva plan includes the Content Planner, you can schedule straight from Canva instead.
Only use photos you took or have rights to, and ask customers before featuring them.

actions.detail: Write captions and image headlines for the week's topics
Save captions alongside the Canva designs
Block 30 minutes to schedule the posts

t: Write a weekly LinkedIn post from your notes
d: Keep a running list of thoughts in Notion and turn the best one into a polished LinkedIn post every week, scheduled ahead.
when: Every Monday morning

steps.h: Set up an ideas page in Notion
steps.b: Create a Notion database called LinkedIn ideas with columns for Idea, Story or example, and Status. Add anything that comes up during your week.

steps.h: Pick one idea and draft it
steps.b: Copy your chosen idea and example into your AI assistant with this prompt. If your Notion plan includes Notion AI you can run it right inside the page.
steps.p: Write a LinkedIn post from this idea: [idea]. Real example from my work: [example]. I am a [job title] who helps [audience]. Structure: a one-line hook that states a surprising point; the story in 3-4 short paragraphs; one practical lesson readers can use today; a closing question. 150-220 words. No emoji, no hashtags in the body, up to 3 hashtags at the end. British English, plain and warm, no buzzwords.

steps.h: Edit it into your own words
steps.b: Change at least one sentence so it sounds like you speaking. Remove anything that names a client without their permission.
When writing a post on LinkedIn, use the clock icon to schedule it for a time your audience is online, such as Tuesday mid-morning. Mark the idea as Posted in Notion.

example: Hook: 'The best proposal I ever wrote was one page long.' Story: a client who skimmed a 20-page deck... Lesson: lead with the decision you need from them. Question: 'What's the shortest document that ever won you work?' #consulting #writing
tips: Keep client stories anonymous unless you have written permission to name them.

actions.detail: Read the newest idea marked Ready in the Notion database
Draft the LinkedIn post
Send the draft to the user to edit and schedule

t: Find the words your customers actually search for
d: A sorted list of 30 to 50 real search phrases for your business, grouped by what people want, ready to use in your website and posts.
when: Before writing web pages or blog posts

steps.b: Type your main service into Google slowly and note the suggestions that drop down, plus the 'People also ask' questions and related searches at the bottom of the results. Try four or five starting phrases.

steps.h: Ask the AI to sort and expand them
steps.b: Paste what you collected into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: I run [business] in [town or region] for [audience]. Here are phrases from Google suggestions and 'People also ask': [paste list]. 1) Remove duplicates. 2) Group them by intent: wants to buy now, comparing options, wants to learn, local search. 3) Add 10 more realistic phrases a customer might type. 4) For each group, suggest one web page or blog post title that would answer them. Output as a table: Phrase, Intent, Suggested page. Don't invent search volumes.

steps.b: Paste the table into Google Sheets and add a column for where you've used each phrase, so you can tick them off.

example: 'emergency plumber near me' (buy now) -> Page: Emergency plumbing in Leeds. 'how much does a boiler service cost' (comparing) -> Post: What a boiler service costs and what's included. 'why is my radiator cold at the top' (learn) -> Post: Cold radiator? Five fixes.
tips: AI can't see real search volumes; if you want numbers, check Google Trends to compare which phrases are more popular.

actions.detail: Group phrases by search intent
Suggest extra phrases and page titles
Save phrases to the keyword sheet

t: Get a plain-English health check of any web page
d: A friendly report on one page of your website: what's clear, what's confusing, and a short fix list to help it show up in search.
when: When a page isn't getting visits or enquiries

steps.b: Open the page, select all the text and copy it. Also note the page title shown in the browser tab and the main phrase you want it to be found for.
Paste the text into your AI assistant with this prompt. Some assistants can read a link directly, but pasting the text is more reliable.
steps.p: Review this web page for a small business. Page title: [title]. Phrase I want it found for: [phrase]. Audience: [who it's for]. Page text: [paste]. Give me: 1) a score out of 10 for clarity and one for search-friendliness, with reasons; 2) whether the main phrase appears in the title, first paragraph and a heading; 3) the three biggest problems a visitor would notice; 4) a rewritten page title (under 60 characters) and meta description (under 155 characters); 5) a numbered fix list, easiest first. Plain English, no jargon.

steps.b: Work through the fix list in your website editor. Most site builders let you change the page title and description in the page's settings or SEO section.

example: Clarity 6/10: the first paragraph talks about your history, not what you do. Search 4/10: 'dog grooming Bristol' isn't in the title or headings. New title: Dog Grooming in Bristol | Gentle, Fear-Free Care. Fix 1: Move prices higher up the page.
tips: Re-run it a month after making changes and compare scores.
Treat it as a second opinion, not a guarantee of rankings.

actions.detail: Read the page text and title
Write the plain-English review and fix list
Save the report

t: Reply to Instagram comments and messages faster
d: A bank of warm, ready-made replies for the questions you get most, saved in Instagram so you can answer in two taps.
when: Set up once, refresh every few months

steps.b: Scroll back through your comments and DMs and write down the ten questions you answer most, like prices, opening hours or delivery.
Paste the list into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: I run [business] on Instagram. Here are the questions people ask most: [list]. For each, write a short reply (under 40 words) that sounds friendly and human, answers the question using these facts: [prices, hours, links, policies], and ends with a light next step. Also give each reply a 1-2 word shortcut name. Format: Shortcut | Reply. British English, no emoji overload (one at most).

steps.b: In Instagram, professional accounts can save replies for messages: look in your settings under Business or Creator tools for saved or quick replies, then add each shortcut and reply.
When you use one, add the person's name or a detail from their message so it never feels copied and pasted.

example: price | Hi! Our cut and finish starts at £38, and colour from £65. Want me to check this week's free slots for you? delivery | We post UK-wide in 2-3 working days, free over £40. Anything I can help you choose?
tips: Never paste customers' private messages into an AI tool with their names or phone numbers; the questions alone are enough.

trigger.detail: New Instagram comment or direct message

actions.detail: Match the message to a common question
Suggest a personalised reply from the saved bank
Show the suggested reply for the user to approve

t: Get a weekly list of trending topics in your niche
d: Every Monday you get five timely post ideas based on what people are talking about in your field, logged in a sheet for planning.
when: Every Monday morning

steps.b: In ChatGPT, if your plan includes scheduled tasks, ask it to run a task every Monday at 8am with the prompt below. It will send you the results as a notification or email.
steps.p: Search the web for what's being discussed this week in [your niche] that matters to [audience] in [country]. Look at news, Google Trends topics and popular questions. Give me 5 post ideas as a table: Topic, Why it's timely (one line, with the source link), Post angle for [business type], Best platform, Suggested first line. Skip anything older than 10 days, and skip sensitive tragedies.

steps.b: No scheduled tasks? Create a recurring Monday event in Google Calendar called 'Trend check' with the prompt pasted in the description, and run it yourself in any AI assistant with web search.
Make a Google Sheet called Trend ideas with the same columns plus Date and Used. Paste each week's table in so you build a bank of ideas over time.
Click the source link for any idea you use. Trends move fast and AI can misread dates.

example: Topic: New rules on garden water butts | Timely: council grants announced Tuesday (link) | Angle: 'How to claim yours in 3 steps' | Instagram carousel | First line: 'Free water butt, anyone?'
tips: Use Google Trends' Explore page to compare two topics quickly before you commit to one.

actions.detail: Search news and trend sources for the niche
Write five timely post ideas with sources
Log the ideas in the Trend ideas sheet
Send the week's ideas to the user

t: Brief yourself on a company before a sales call
d: A one-page snapshot of a prospect's recent posts, news, tone and likely priorities, with three smart questions to open the call.
when: Before every sales or partnership call

steps.b: Skim the company's LinkedIn page and website news for the last month. Copy the text of three to five recent posts or announcements.
Paste the posts into an AI assistant with web search turned on and use this prompt.
steps.p: I have a call with [company name] ([website]) about [what you offer]. Here are their recent posts and news: [paste]. Also search for any recent public news about them. Give me: 1) a 3-sentence summary of what they're focused on right now; 2) their tone and what they seem proud of; 3) likely challenges they might have that relate to [your offer]; 4) three open questions I could ask early in the call; 5) anything to avoid mentioning. Mark anything you're unsure of as 'unconfirmed'. One page max.

steps.b: Paste the brief into the calendar invite's notes or your notes app so it's in front of you when the call starts.

example: Focus: opening a second site in Manchester and hiring 20 staff. Tone: proud of their apprentices. Likely challenge: training new staff quickly. Ask: 'How are you getting new starters up to speed for the Manchester opening?' Avoid: last year's product recall (unconfirmed).
tips: Stick to public, business information. Don't dig into individuals' personal social accounts.

trigger.detail: One hour before a meeting tagged sales

actions.detail: Read the company's recent public posts and news
Write the one-page call brief
Send the brief to the user

t: Turn a blog post into a swipeable carousel
d: Your existing article becomes a 7 to 10 slide Instagram or LinkedIn carousel with a hook, clear points and a final call to action.
when: After publishing a new article

steps.b: Paste your article into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Turn this article into a carousel of [7-10] slides for [Instagram or LinkedIn]. Article: [paste]. Slide 1: a hook of max 8 words that promises a clear benefit. Slides 2 to second-last: one idea each, a headline of max 6 words and a supporting line of max 20 words. Last slide: a call to action to [read the full post, follow, book]. Also write a caption of under 80 words. Output as a numbered list. Keep facts exactly as in the article.

steps.h: Pick a carousel template in Canva
steps.b: Search Canva for 'carousel' and choose a template in the right size (square or portrait 4:5). Swap in your brand colours and fonts.
Paste each slide's text in, keeping it big and readable on a phone. Download as PNGs for Instagram, or as a PDF for a LinkedIn document post.
Upload the slides in order and add the caption. Link to the full article in your bio or the first comment.

example: Slide 1: 'Five mistakes that slow down your laptop'. Slide 2: 'Too many startup apps' / 'Every app that opens at login eats memory before you've started.' ... Slide 8: 'Want the full checklist? Link in bio.'
tips: Make one carousel template once and duplicate it each time to keep a consistent look.

trigger.detail: New article added to the blog folder

actions.detail: Write carousel slide text and caption
Save the slide text for designing in Canva
Tell the user the carousel copy is ready

t: Write a full launch pack for a new product
d: One brief becomes a launch email, a week of social posts and a short announcement for your website, all saying the same thing.
when: Two weeks before a launch or sale

steps.b: Cover what it is, who it's for, the price, the launch date and the one reason someone should care. This keeps every piece consistent.
Paste your brief into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Using this launch brief: [brief], write a launch pack for [business]. 1) Email: 3 subject line options (under 45 characters), a preview line, and a 150-word email with one button label. 2) Five social posts for the launch week: teaser (3 days before), launch day, customer benefit, behind the scenes, last chance. Each under 70 words with an image idea. 3) A 60-word website banner announcement. Keep the price, date and claims exactly as in the brief. British English, warm, no hype words.

steps.b: Paste everything into a Google Doc so you can check it, share it with anyone helping, and fix any detail in one place.
Create a new email campaign in Mailchimp, paste in the text, pick a subject line and schedule it for launch morning.
Add the five posts to your scheduler or a calendar reminder for each day of launch week.

example: Subject: 'Our winter blend is back'. Email: 'It sold out in nine days last year...' Teaser post: 'Something warm is coming Thursday.' Banner: 'Winter Blend returns 14 Nov - pre-order now, £9.50 a bag.'
tips: Only send emails to people who signed up to hear from you, and keep the unsubscribe link Mailchimp adds.

trigger.detail: User fills in the launch brief form

actions.detail: Write email, social posts and banner text
Create the launch pack document
Add a reminder for each launch-week post

t: Turn customer reviews into social proof posts
d: Your best reviews become eye-catching quote graphics and captions that show new customers why people love you.
when: Once a month

steps.b: Copy five to ten recent reviews from Google, your shop or emails. Use only the reviewer's first name or initials.
Paste the reviews into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Here are customer reviews for [business]: [paste reviews, first names only]. 1) Pick the 5 most persuasive and pull out a short quote from each (max 20 words, using their exact words, no changes to meaning). 2) For each, note which worry it answers for a new customer (price, quality, trust, speed...). 3) Write a caption for each (under 50 words) that adds context and ends with a gentle call to action. Output as a numbered list: Quote | Name | Worry answered | Caption.

steps.b: In Canva, search for a 'testimonial' or 'quote' template, add the quote and first name, and duplicate it for the others so they match.
Post one a week. Check the reviewer is happy to be featured if the review came from a private email.

example: Quote: 'They fixed in an hour what another firm couldn't in a week.' - Priya | Worry: speed | Caption: 'When your laptop dies the day before a deadline, every hour counts. Book a same-day repair through the link in bio.'
tips: Never edit a quote to say something the customer didn't; shortening is fine, rewording isn't.

actions.detail: Pull the best short quotes from new reviews
Write a caption for each quote
Add four quote posts to the month's content list

t: Plan seasonal posts for a local trade business
d: A season's worth of useful tips, reminders and offers for a local trade like a garage, plumber or gardener, with matching images ready to schedule.
when: At the start of each season

steps.h: Note what customers need this season
steps.b: Write down the jobs that spike this time of year (for a garage: winter tyres, batteries, MOTs) and any offers you want to push.

steps.h: Ask for a season of posts
steps.b: Paste this into your AI assistant.
steps.p: I run a [trade] business in [town]. The next 12 weeks are [season]. Common jobs now: [list]. Offers: [list]. Write 12 weekly social posts: mostly practical tips customers can do themselves, plus 3 offers and 2 'meet the team' posts. For each: week number, headline for the image (max 6 words), caption (50-80 words, local and friendly), call to action (call, book online, pop in), and a photo idea I can take on my phone. British English.

steps.h: Snap the photos on your phone
steps.b: Take a batch of photos in one go at work: your van, tools, team and finished jobs. Ask team members before photographing them.
Drop each photo into one Canva template with the headline on top, then duplicate for each week.
Use Meta Business Suite to schedule all 12 to Facebook and Instagram, or add a weekly reminder to post them yourself.

example: Week 3: 'Is your battery winter ready?' Caption: 'Cold mornings are hard on car batteries. If your engine sounds sluggish, pop in to our Station Road garage for a free 5-minute test.' Photo: tester clipped to a battery.
tips: Blur or crop out customer number plates and house numbers in job photos.

actions.detail: Write 12 weeks of seasonal posts and photo ideas
Add the posts to the content calendar

t: Get a monthly social media results summary
d: A one-page summary of what worked on your social accounts last month, what didn't, and three changes to try next month.
when: First working day of each month

steps.b: Open the insights or analytics area of each platform (Instagram, Facebook via Meta Business Suite, LinkedIn page analytics). Note reach, engagement and follows for each post, or export them if the platform offers a download.
Paste them into a Google Sheet with columns: Date, Platform, Post topic, Format, Reach, Likes, Comments, Shares, Saves, Link clicks.
Copy the table into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Here are last month's social media results for [business]: [paste table]. Our goal is [goal, e.g. bookings, website visits]. Give me: 1) a 3-sentence overview; 2) the top 3 posts and what they have in common (topic, format, timing); 3) the weakest 3 and a likely reason; 4) month-on-month change if I've included last month; 5) three specific experiments for next month. Use only the numbers given; don't invent any. Plain English, one page.

steps.b: Pick one of the experiments and add it to next month's content calendar.

example: Overview: reach up 18%, but link clicks flat. Top posts were all short videos posted before 9am. Weakest: three offer posts with stock images. Try: film two behind-the-scenes clips a week; post offers with real photos; test a Tuesday 8am slot.
tips: Keep every month in the same sheet on separate tabs so you can ask the assistant to spot trends over a quarter.

actions.detail: Remind the user to export last month's numbers
Summarise results and suggest experiments
Save the monthly results summary

t: Run a weekly social posting routine on autopilot
d: A repeatable system where ideas in a sheet become drafted captions, branded images and scheduled posts each week with very little effort.
when: Set up once, then 30 minutes every Friday

steps.b: In Google Sheets, create columns: Week, Topic, Headline, Caption, Hashtags, Status. Add 10 or more topics you could post about. Share it with anyone who has ideas.
If your ChatGPT plan includes scheduled tasks, set a weekly Friday task with this prompt and paste in the week's topics; otherwise run it yourself from a recurring Friday calendar event.
steps.p: For [business], a [type] serving [audience], write posts for these topics: [paste topics]. For each give: Headline (max 6 words), Caption (50-80 words, one call to action: [CTA]), 3-5 Hashtags. Output as a table with columns Topic | Headline | Caption | Hashtags so I can paste it straight into Google Sheets. British English, warm, no hype.

steps.b: Paste the table into the matching columns and set Status to Drafted. Edit anything that doesn't sound like you.

steps.h: Make all the images at once
steps.b: If your Canva plan includes Bulk Create, connect the sheet's Headline column to a template to make every image in one go. Otherwise duplicate one template and paste each headline.
Schedule the posts in Meta Business Suite, LinkedIn or Canva's Content Planner, then set Status to Scheduled. Your Friday calendar event keeps the routine going.

example: Friday 3pm: 5 topics pulled from the sheet -> captions drafted -> 5 matching images from Bulk Create -> posts queued Mon to Fri at 8am. Sheet now shows Week 46: 5 Scheduled, 3 ideas left in the bank.
tips: Top up the idea bank whenever a customer asks a good question; that's your best source of topics.
Check every drafted post before it goes out; never fully skip the human read-through.

actions.detail: Read next week's topics from the idea sheet
Write headline, caption and hashtags for each
Fill in drafts and set status to Drafted
Ask the user to review, make images and schedule

t: Post a fresh Google Business Profile update every week
d: Short, local updates for your Google Business Profile that keep your listing active and tell nearby customers what's new.
when: Every week

steps.b: Snap a recent job, product, dish or your team at work. Real photos tend to do better than stock images.
Paste this into your AI assistant to get a month's worth.
steps.p: Write 4 Google Business Profile updates for [business] in [town]. What's happening this month: [news, offers, events, seasonal services]. Each update: 60-100 words, mentions the local area naturally, describes one specific thing (a job, offer or event), and ends with a clear action that matches a button: Call, Book, Learn more or Order online. Avoid phone numbers and links in the text. British English, friendly and plain.

steps.b: Search your business name on Google or open the Google Business Profile app while signed in, choose to add an update, add the photo and text, and pick the matching button.

d: Each time you add a product to your Shopify store, you get a ready caption, hashtags and a photo idea to announce it.

steps.b: From the product page in your Shopify admin, copy the title, description, price and any key details like sizes or materials.

t: Draft a blog post from a few keywords
d: Start with three or four keywords and end with an outlined, fully drafted blog post in Google Docs, ready for your own edit.
when: Whenever you need a new article

steps.b: Write down the main phrase you want to be found for, two or three related phrases, and who the article is for.
Ask for the outline before the full draft so you can steer it. Paste this into your AI assistant.
steps.p: I'm writing a blog post for [business or blog name]. Reader: [who they are and what they're struggling with]. Main keyword: [phrase]. Related phrases: [list]. Suggest 3 title options (under 60 characters, main keyword near the start) and an outline with an intro, 4-6 H2 headings, a short bullet list under each of what to cover, and a conclusion with a call to action to [action]. Note any facts or figures I'll need to check or supply.

steps.h: Adjust, then ask for the draft
steps.b: Change the outline as you like, then reply: 'Write the full post from this outline, 900-1,200 words, in a friendly, expert tone, short paragraphs, British English. Use my own examples where I've marked them.'
Paste the draft into a Google Doc. Add your own stories, opinions and photos; that is what makes it worth reading and stops it sounding generic.

example: Title: Garden Office Planning Permission: What You Need to Know. H2s: Do you need permission at all? The 2.5 metre rule. Listed buildings and conservation areas. How to check with your council. What we do for you. CTA: Book a free site survey.
tips: Check every fact, rule or statistic the draft includes against an official source before publishing.

actions.detail: Suggest titles and an outline
Write the full draft from the approved outline
Create a Google Doc with the draft

t: Teach your AI assistant to write like you
d: A personal style guide built from your own writing that you can reuse so every draft sounds like you, not like a robot.
when: Set up once, update every few months

steps.b: Pick three pieces you've written and like: an email, a post and something longer. Remove other people's names and private details.

steps.h: Ask it to describe your style
steps.b: Paste the samples into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Here are three samples of my writing: [paste samples]. Analyse my style and write a voice guide I can reuse. Include: 1) tone in 5 words; 2) typical sentence length and rhythm; 3) words and phrases I use often; 4) words I never seem to use; 5) how I open and close pieces; 6) how I use humour, questions or lists; 7) 5 do's and 5 don'ts. Then rewrite this paragraph in my voice to test it: [a generic paragraph].

steps.h: Save the guide where you'll reuse it

steps.b: Note your brand colours, the mood you want and two or three images you like the style of (described in words, not copied).
Ask your AI assistant for a reusable style description, then use it for every image. ChatGPT and Gemini can create images directly; Canva's AI image tools work too.
steps.p: Create a reusable image style description for [business], whose brand feels [3 words] with colours [colours]. The style should suit [use: social posts, blog headers]. Give me: a one-paragraph style recipe (medium, lighting, colour palette, composition, level of detail, what to avoid). Then use it to create an image of: [first subject]. steps.h: Make the rest in the same chat

steps.b: Open your AI assistant and attach up to a handful of photos at once.

steps.b: Paste this prompt alongside the photos.

t: Turn a podcast episode into show notes and clips
d: From one episode transcript, get show notes, chapter times, quotable moments and a list of short clips worth cutting for social.

steps.b: Use the transcript from your recording or hosting tool, or upload the episode to YouTube as unlisted and copy the automatic captions from YouTube Studio.

steps.h: Ask for show notes and clip picks
steps.b: Paste the transcript into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Here's the transcript of my podcast episode: [paste]. Show: [name] for [audience]. Guest: [name, if any]. Give me: 1) 3 episode title options; 2) show notes: a 100-word summary and 5 bullet key takeaways; 3) chapter markers with timestamps; 4) 5 clips of 30-60 seconds for social media, each with start and end time, why it works on its own, and a hook line for on-screen text; 5) 3 short quotes, word for word. t: Turn a rambling voice note into tasks and events
d: Talk through your week on a walk, and get back a tidy to-do list plus calendar events for anything with a date or time.
when: Whenever your head is full

steps.b: Use your phone's voice recorder and just talk: what you need to do, who to call, deadlines, ideas. Many phones now transcribe recordings automatically (for example Voice Memos on recent iPhones or Recorder on Pixel).

steps.h: Get the text into your assistant
steps.b: Copy the transcript, or upload the audio file to an AI assistant that accepts audio. You can also speak directly using the assistant's voice mode.
Use this prompt.
steps.p: Here's a transcript of me thinking out loud: [paste]. Today is [day and date]. Sort it into: 1) Tasks, each starting with a verb, with a suggested due date if I mentioned one, grouped by Work, Home, Errands; 2) Calendar events with title, date, start time and length (only if I said a time or day); 3) Ideas to keep; 4) anything unclear I should decide. Don't add tasks I didn't mention.

steps.b: Add the events to Google Calendar and the tasks to your reminders app. If your assistant is connected to Google Calendar (Gemini can be), you can ask it to create the events for you, then check them.

example: Work: Send Lucy the revised quote (Tue). Home: Book boiler service. Errands: Return parcel to the post office. Events: Dentist, Thu 14 Nov 9:30, 45 mins. Ideas: Winter newsletter about energy saving. Unclear: 'sort the van' - service or clean?
tips: Don't record other people's conversations without their knowledge; this is for your own voice.

Add tasks to the reminders list

t: Understand voice messages in another language
d: A voice message in a language you don't speak becomes a clear English translation, plus a reply you can send back in their language.
when: When you get a voice note you can't understand

steps.b: WhatsApp can transcribe voice messages if you turn on transcripts in its settings (supported languages vary). Otherwise, play it near an AI assistant in voice mode, or forward the audio file to an assistant that accepts audio.
Paste the transcript into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: This is a transcript of a voice message I received, probably in [language, or 'unknown']: [paste]. 1) Tell me which language it is. 2) Translate it into English, keeping the tone. 3) Note anything ambiguous or culturally important. 4) Write a short, polite reply in that language saying: [what you want to say], and give me the English version so I know what I'm sending.

steps.b: Send the reply as text, or read it aloud and record a voice note if you're confident.

example: Language: Portuguese. Translation: 'Hi, it's Ana from the flat downstairs. The water's been dripping through my ceiling since this morning. Can you check your bathroom?' Reply: 'Olá Ana, desculpe! Vou verificar agora e falo consigo em 10 minutos.'
tips: Voice messages are personal; avoid sharing ones with sensitive details, and for anything legal or medical, use a professional translator.

actions.detail: Transcribe and detect the language
Translate and draft a reply in the same language
Show the translation and suggested reply

t: Make a narrated explainer video in Canva
d: A short slideshow-style video with your own voiceover, captions and music, made in Canva from an AI-written script.
when: When you need to explain something simply

steps.b: Paste this into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Write a script for a [60-90]-second explainer video about [topic] for [audience]. Split it into 6-8 scenes. For each scene: the voiceover (max 25 words, plain spoken English), a short on-screen headline (max 6 words), and a visual idea that I can make in Canva with icons, photos or simple shapes. End with a call to action: [CTA].

steps.b: Start a Canva video design, add one page per scene, and use templates, icons and your own photos. Add the headlines as big, readable text.
Use Canva's record option to narrate each page, or record on your phone's voice recorder in a quiet room and upload the audio. Your own voice builds more trust than a synthetic one.
Turn on Canva's auto captions if offered on your plan, or type the voiceover as text. Pick a quiet track from Canva's audio library.
Download as MP4 and upload to YouTube, your website or social channels.

example: Scene 1: 'Recycling bins confusing? You're not alone.' Visual: three coloured bins. Scene 3: 'Rinse it, squash it, lid on.' Visual: icon sequence. Scene 7: 'Download the bin calendar at our website.' Final: 75 seconds, captions on.
tips: Only use music, photos and footage you have the rights to; Canva's library is licensed for use in your designs, subject to its terms.
If you include anyone else's face or voice, get their permission first.

actions.detail: Write a scene-by-scene script with visuals
Save the script for building in Canva
Book 45 minutes to build and record

t: Film a month of short videos in one session
d: Plan, film and schedule eight or more short videos from one afternoon of filming, spread across the month on YouTube Shorts and Reels.
when: Once a month

steps.b: Ask your AI assistant for a set of scripts that can all be filmed in one place.
steps.p: Plan [8] short vertical videos (20-45 seconds) for [business/channel] about [topics], aimed at [audience]. All must be filmable in [location] in one afternoon with one phone. For each: title, 2-second hook, 3-5 shot script with spoken lines, props needed, and outfit changes if any. Then give a filming order that groups videos by setup to save time, and a posting schedule of 2 a week.

steps.b: Gather the props list, set up near good light, and film in the suggested order. Name each clip with the video number as you go.
Edit all the videos in one sitting in your phone's editor or Canva, using the same caption style and ending.
Upload to YouTube Studio and set each to Schedule with a date and time. For Instagram, schedule Reels in Meta Business Suite or the Instagram app if your account offers scheduling.
Add a recurring monthly event to Google Calendar for your filming afternoon.

example: Filming order: kitchen counter (videos 1, 4, 6), garden (2, 7), front door (3, 5, 8). Schedule: Tue and Fri at 6pm through November. Total: 8 Shorts, 3 hours filming, 2 hours editing.
tips: Film a few extra hooks for each video; you can swap them later if one doesn't perform.

steps.h: Set up folders and a tracker
steps.b: Create Google Drive folders: To upload, Uploaded. Make a Google Sheet with columns: Video file, Title, Playlist, Publish date, Status.
Ask your AI assistant to suggest playlists from your video list.
steps.p: Here's a list of my YouTube videos and their topics: [paste titles]. My channel is about [topic] for [audience]. Put each video in at least one playlist.

steps.b: In YouTube Studio, create each playlist with its description. When uploading new videos, you can choose the playlist on the details screen.

steps.b: For each finished video in To upload, upload it in YouTube Studio, set visibility to Schedule, add it to its playlist, then move the file to Uploaded and update the sheet.

t: Check product photos meet listing rules before uploading
d: A quick pass or fail on every product photo against marketplace rules and your own standards, with what to fix on any that fail.
when: Before uploading product photos

steps.b: List the rules for where you sell (for example plain background, product fills most of the frame, no added text) plus your own standards like lighting and angles. Check the marketplace's help pages for its current image rules.
Attach a batch of photos to your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Check each attached product photo against this checklist: [paste checklist]. For each photo, in order, give: Photo number | Pass or Fail | Which rules it fails | What exactly to fix (e.g. 'reshoot with more light from the left', 'crop tighter'). Then a one-line summary of the most common problem across the batch. Be strict but only judge what you can see.

steps.b: Reshoot or edit the failures, then run the check again on the new versions before uploading.

tips: AI can miss small details like a faint watermark or a scratch, so give each photo a final look yourself at full size.

t: Run a weekly video production line for your channel
d: A repeatable weekly system that takes each video from idea to scheduled upload, with AI help, shared folders and automatic reminders.

steps.b: Use Trello's built-in automation to add due dates and checklists when cards move, for example 'when moved to Filmed, add checklist: back up footage, rough cut, captions, thumbnail'.
